1014-the-lure-of-the-dim-trails:
B. M. Bower wrote this western about the lure of the dim trails, opening with a search for the western tone. Reeve-Howard, an artist of dry-point etchings, asks a friend why he worries that a mere pastime fails to pay, since he does not depend on the work for a living. The friend, a writer, seeks a truer West.

Bower follows the pair through ranch country, where art, work, and romance test their ideas of the frontier. Her prose is warm and knowledgeable, with the West as both a place and a dream. The book suits readers who like westerns about the West itself, and about those who chase its fading trails.
19701-health-work-in-the-public-schools:
Health Work in the Public Schools argues that schools must guard children's bodies too. Its key tool is medical inspection of pupils. The book says educator and physician should join hands in the school. Their shared aim is health strong enough for children to use free schooling well. Inspection, in its words, safeguards children from disease.

School health work was a young field when this guide appeared. Reformers saw crowded classrooms spreading sickness fast. A doctor's eye in school could catch what teachers missed. The book lays out that case in plain, hopeful terms. It also promises healthier, happier, more vigorous children. Modern school nursing grew from arguments exactly like these.
19850-the-human-side-of-animals:
Royal Dixon wrote The Human Side of Animals in 1918. It argues that animals show traits we call human. One odd claim stars the porcupine and the hedgehog. After shaking down berries or grapes, they roll in them. Then they hurry home with food stuck to their quills. Dixon reports such tales with warm sympathy for animal minds.

Popular natural history then loved animal intelligence stories. Dixon collected anecdotes of memory, affection, and cunning. Science has since tested many such claims hard. Some of Dixon's travelers' tales will not survive testing. The book still shows the era's animal feeling. It helped build public kindness toward wildlife.
19896-queer-stories-for-boys-and-girls:
Queer Stories for Boys and Girls gathers Edward Abbott Parry's odd tales. Parry explains this is their first fair book issue. Earlier editions fell into the hands of freebooters, he complains. He had to pay a round sum for the plates to free his tales. Queer here means strange and whimsical, not anything else. The stories mix nonsense, fairies, and upside-down logic.

Parry was a judge who wrote children's fantasy on the side. His tales play with words, animals, and polite absurdity. Piracy of popular books was a real author's grievance then. His preface's anger is part of the period record. The stories themselves stay light on their feet. Young readers got wit without a single sermon.
20081-a-houseful-of-girls:
Sarah Tytler wrote A Houseful of Girls, a novel of a home full of young women. The book notes a strange, quick bond among girls on the edge of womanhood. They catch looks and whispers meant to pass over their heads. Blushes, shrugs, and quick glances spread through the group at once.

Tytler writes of sisters, friends, and the small storms of a full house. Each girl reads the others with sharp, shared instinct. The tale turns on youth, love, and family strain. Readers get a warm, keen look at girlhood as one writer of the era saw it.
20260-daybreak-a-story-for-girls:
Florence A. Sitwell wrote Daybreak, a story for girls with a gentle, devout tone. A woman reads Milton's Ode on the Morning of Christ's Nativity. She lays the book aside only as small feet gather at her door. Clear, passionless voices then blend in a Christmas hymn outside.

That calm scene sets the mood for a tale of girls and faith. Daybreak, as a title, promises new light after doubt or sorrow. Sitwell writes of home, school, and inner growth with quiet care. Young readers get a soft, uplifting story in the Victorian girls' tradition.
20424-a-son-of-the-hills:
A Son of the Hills, published in 1913, is a novel of the American hill country. Its people trace their roots back to the days of the Revolution. The book insists that the hill folk of that age were of the best stock in the land.

All who could serve their country then, the story says, did it nobly and well. Some signed the Declaration of Independence and then went home with dignity to their hills. The novel builds its tale of love and hardship on that proud heritage, and on the stubborn ways of families who answer to no one.
20475-the-two-admirals:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote The Two Admirals as a sea novel of the age of sail. Two old admirals, friends and rivals, command fleets in wartime. Cooper had served in the navy himself, and his battle scenes rest on hard knowledge of ships and seamanship.

He explains that a fleet's power is bound by its slowest ship. The efficiency of a fleet, he writes, is confined to the rate of sailing of its dullest member. Winds and currents rule every plan an admiral makes. The novel pairs that stern sea craft with a story of honor between two aging commanders.
20499-afloat-or-adventures-on-watery-tra:
Afloat, or Adventures on Watery Trails, published in 1917, is a boys' outdoor adventure. A group of friends finds a couple of weeks of vacation still ahead of them. Toby speaks for the rest: it would be a shame to let the good old summer dribble away.

One more whack at the woods and the open air is what they want. The boys take to boats and trails, camping and fishing as they go. The book belongs to the row of summer adventure stories that taught city boys to prize canoes, campfires, and self-reliance.
20557-ontario-teachers-manuals-household:
This Ontario teachers' manual aims to bring household science into rural schools across the province. Household science covered cooking, sewing, health, and the running of a home. The manual was issued to encourage its introduction and further its progress.

The need was large. The manual counts 903 urban schools against 5,697 rural schools in Ontario. Rural pupils made up nearly forty-six percent of the school population. Lessons therefore had to suit one-room schools and farm homes. The manual shows how governments of the day tried to carry modern home training into the countryside.
20633-winsome-winnie-and-other-new-nonse:
Stephen Leacock's Winsome Winnie and Other New Nonsense Novels parodies the popular fiction of his day. Leacock, the Canadian humorist, wrote each short novel as a burlesque of a familiar type. Sob stories, sea tales, and society novels all get the treatment.

The contents list alone raises a laugh. Has Anybody Here Seen Kelly? stands beside Show Me the Man Who Wore Those Boots. The Kidnapped Plumber is billed as a tale of the new timberland. Broken Barriers offers red love on a blue island. Leacock's nonsense novels remain models of the parody form.
20775-the-annals-of-the-cakchiquels:
The Annals of the Cakchiquels record the past of a Maya people of highland Guatemala. The translator worked straight from the source text, owning his own errors. He thanks the late Abbe Brasseur, a famed student of native America, for a prior draft.

Kings, wars, migrations, and rites unfold in the Cakchiquel's own telling. Few native histories from the colonial age survive in such full form. Daniel Brinton, who brought this text to English readers, prized such sources. The annals let a conquered people speak of their own past in their own order and voice.
20918-auld-licht-idylls:
Hens roost on kitchen rafters among staves and fishing rods in Auld Licht Idylls. J. M. Barrie's 1896 sketches show a thrift-driven home that took hens indoors. Meal times strew the hearth with feathers, yet the birds give little true trouble.

The Auld Lichts, a strict Scots church sect, fill Barrie's tales of Thrums life. Elders, weavers, and widows move through sketches warm with wry pity. Barrie drew on his mother's tales of old Kirriemuir for this world. The book made his early fame and still shows how deftly he mixed humour and pathos in small-town Scots life.
20963-grandmother-dear-a-book-for-boys-a:
Three children stand mute, each hiding a view on the matter at hand in Grandmother Dear. Mrs. Molesworth opens her book for boys and girls on that shy deadlock. Each waits to learn the others' minds before risking a word.

Molesworth, a queen of Victorian children's tales, centres a wise, loved grandmother here. Home trials, small faults, and mended ways fill her gentle plot. Her tales taught by example, with talk as true as life. Grandmother Dear shows her art at its best: no shouting morals, just a home whose love slowly sets young hearts right.
21109-big-game-a-story-for-girls:
Margot's brother Ron wants to be a poet, but their father insists he should take a proper job in the family firm. In Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's story for girls, Margot schemes to get Ron's poems published and change their father's mind. She learns that a poetry magazine editor holidays at a remote Scottish Highlands hotel.

She books them into the same hotel, whose landlady dislikes women guests. Fishing trips and a long walk in bad weather follow, and Margot catches pneumonia after getting Ron near the editor. Back in London the truth about her own admirer surprises her, and one of Ron's poems does reach print.
21120-the-fortunes-of-the-farrells:
Old Bernard Farrell is immensely rich, long unseen by his family, and suddenly in need of care. Visiting relatives take him in for a few days. He proposes that his nephews and nieces come stay with him in turn, so he can judge who should inherit most of his wealth.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey gathers the young people at his house, where he proves an unpleasant host. He has made a secret early will in case of accident, and the guests burn to read it. Someone does peek at his desk, and Farrell demands the truth at his bedside. Vaizey keeps the answer back for the end.
21121-a-houseful-of-girls:
Six big girls live in a big house on a long road. The road runs out of London into Hertfordshire, in Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's Edwardian novel. Christabel, the youngest, keeps a picture of John Gilpin on her wall because his famous ride passed down that road. Each sister meets life in her own way.

Engagements made and broken set the sisters reacting differently to the same news, which is the book's chief pleasure. Friends and suitors move through the houseful of girls as they grow up. Vaizey, also known as Jessie Mansergh, writes family talk and sisterly loyalty with an easy, amused touch throughout.
21213-new-ideals-in-rural-schools:
George Herbert Betts, a professor of psychology at Cornell College in Iowa, wrote this 1913 volume in the Riverside Educational Monographs series. Rural schools, he argues, face the same problem as any school: giving the community the largest return on its investment with the least waste. He calls schools great education factories working on raw material.

Four chapters treat the rural school's problem, its social organisation, its curriculum, and its teaching. Betts wants country schools fitted to farm life rather than copied from city models. The book belongs to the country life movement that tried to keep rural communities strong through better schooling.
21223-the-carbonels:
Summer 1822 opens Charlotte M. Yonge's novel in a shabby garden. A lawyer in a green coat delivers his verdict on the Uphill people: a bad lot, good for nothing and ungrateful. The Carbonel family has just arrived to live among them. Military dress, white dresses, and a tall old gig set the period.

Yonge follows the Carbonels as newcomers in a country parish where opinion is already fixed against their poorer neighbours. The story tests that first harsh judgement against daily knowledge of the people condemned. Village talk, church life, and family duty fill the chapters. It is quieter than her historical tales, and firmly rooted in place.
21229-thistle-and-rose-a-story-for-girls:
Anna is fifteen, motherless, and about to travel alone for the first time in Amy Walton's story for girls. Her father must go abroad on business, so Anna goes to Dornton while he is away. She looks forward to meeting relatives there, including a grandfather long estranged from her father.

The old man lives quietly with no servants and works as organist at Dornton church. He is known as a fine music teacher, above all of the violin. Anna's stay opens the way between father and grandfather. Walton keeps the tale short and warm, with music, first journeys, and family healing at its heart.
21447-the-three-admirals:
Old friends rise to the top of the navy in W. H. G. Kingston's The Three Admirals. The book closes a set of four that begins with The Three Midshipmen. It shows life in the Royal Navy of the 1860s, as the three men reach flag rank.

The corvette Dragon, once led by their friend Jack Rogers, crosses the wide Pacific in one strand. She sails from Japan toward Esquimalt harbour on Vancouver's Island with dispatches. The three admirals also visit the grave of Admiral Triton on the Isle of Wight. Service, travel, and loyalty tie this long last volume together.
21608-the-dawn-of-reason-or-mental-trait:
James Weir, a doctor of medicine, argues that animals think in The Dawn of Reason, published in 1899. His full title adds Mental Traits in the Lower Animals. Weir dedicated the book to his father, no scientist, who yet followed the work with keen interest.

Chapters begin with conscious and unconscious mind, traced from jellyfish upward. The senses of touch, taste, and smell in low animals come next. Weir ties body, form, and mind into one chain of growth. His cases of clever beasts test where instinct ends and reason starts, a live question in the age after Darwin.
21666-uncle-rutherford-s-nieces-a-story-:
Joanna H. Mathews writes for girls in Uncle Rutherford's Nieces, copyrighted in 1888. A rustic seat, built by the devoted Jim, tips unless its riders balance exactly. The nieces' small dog lies at their feet as the tale opens.

Chapters promise an arithmetical puzzle, a cablegram, and food for the gods. A morning bugle, Uncle Rutherford's prize, and two peanut sellers follow. Mathews, author of the Bessie Books, fills the tale with home fun and small trials. Stokes of New York published it with original pictures, dedicated to a boy named Herbert Hunt on his birthday.
21835-the-jew-and-american-ideals:
Anti-Semitism in America is John Spargo's target in this 1921 Harper book, written by a socialist thinker who knew the radical world from inside. Spargo begins with his own story. Five years earlier he was invited to join a rich manufacturer's plan to end the war by Christmas. His chapters then take up the alleged great Jewish conspiracy and the mystery of the Protocols.

He asks whether socialism is a Jewish plot, studies Jewish socialists and Bolshevism, and calls anti-Semitism itself a vicious force. The close pleads for the cooperation of Christian and Jew in American life. Spargo writes as a debater with documents in hand. The book is a notable early American answer to a rising poison.
21857-joyce-s-investments-a-story-for-gi:
A young heiress puts her money to work for a factory village in Joyce's Investments, a story for girls by Fannie E. Newberry, published in 1899. Joyce Lavillotte is not yet twenty-two, but she has been motherless long and knows her own mind. The factory may be the manager's province, she tells the lawyer, but the village shall be hers. Her investments are people.

Chapters follow her among the cottages, into a social house she builds, and through sorrow, a lock-up visit, and a railroad wedding. The motto on the title page praises woman's genius of charity. Newberry writes reform as a girl's adventure. Joyce's bright eyes and firm will carry a serious plan: wealth spent on neighbors, face to face.
21876-mary-louise-and-the-liberty-girls:
American girls organize for war work in Mary Louise and the Liberty Girls, by Edith Van Dyne, published in 1918. Van Dyne's preface says the tale means to show what large tasks girls can do when spurred by patriotism. Liberty Girls, she urges, can form in every city and hamlet, useful in peace as in war. Charity toward all and malice toward none is her second message.

Mary Louise takes command at a mass meeting, opens a Liberty Shop, and hunts a traitor through hints, explosions, and a black satchel. Josie, the detective's daughter, brings the professional touch. Edith Van Dyne was a pen name of L. Frank Baum, the Oz author. The book is wartime series fiction with a patriotic heart and a mystery plot.
21973-anecdotes-of-the-habits-and-instin:
Animal cleverness is collected story by story in Mrs. R. Lee's Anecdotes of the Habits and Instinct of Animals, published at London in 1852. Lee, formerly Mrs. Bowdich, had written on Africa and Australia and a memoir of Cuvier. In her preface she says the material crowded in beyond all her plans. Much was new, or stamped true by friends who drew on private stores. Harrison Weir drew the pictures, a monkey painter among them.

Dry details of science and classification are laid aside, she promises, though a loose order is kept. Dogs, elephants, birds, and beasts of every kind act out their natures in short tales. The book belongs to the age when natural history was taught by anecdote. Its charm is its faith that animals have characters worth watching.
22164-a-modern-tomboy-a-story-for-girls:
Mrs. L. T. Meade, one of the most prolific girls' writers of her age, published A Modern Tomboy as a story for girls. It opens with a new school: Mrs. Merriman and Lucy stand ready to receive their pupils. Talk runs on the new girls, and one name charms everyone in advance. "Phyllis Flower" sounds too sweet, Lucy declares, and she knows she will fall in love with its owner.

The tomboy of the title upsets the school's smooth ways. Meade builds her tales on character, discipline, and girls learning to judge each other fairly. Hundreds of her books filled school prize lists. This one shows her formula at its most characteristic.
22309-an-american-robinson-crusoe-for-am:
An American Robinson Crusoe retells the famous castaway story for American boys and girls. The catalog notes it as an adaptation, with added incidents. Its preface explains why the old tale was reshaped for schools.

The adapter drew on many years of work with the story in early grades. The book was made for use in elementary classrooms. Its aim was to teach how human progress begins and grows. A lone survivor building a life from nothing made that lesson vivid. Generations of children met Crusoe this way, in a version sized and shaped for young readers.
22363-the-country-of-the-neutrals:
The Country of the Neutrals traces a region from Champlain to Talbot, per its subtitle. Old map notes anchor much of the account. One marks where the Neutral Nation formerly stood.

West of Burlington Bay, a map calls the land good. On the Niagara River, it warns the current can hardly be ascended. At the river's mouth, Native reports put Niagara Falls above two hundred feet. Lake Ontario's south side is drawn, the writer says, pretty accurately. Such scraps rebuild a lost geography of the lakes. Readers get early Canada and New York border country through maps, names, and memory.
22396-king-arthur-s-knights-the-tales-re:
Henry Gilbert retold King Arthur's Knights for boys and girls. The tales open with King Uther Pendragon dying in London. He lies in his Roman palace, long sick with a wasting disease.

Uther gnaws his beard with wrath at his own weakness. Meanwhile, pagan Saxons ravage the broad lands of Britain. They leave smoking ruin, broken towns, and desolated villages behind. Mothers lie dead beside their children on the hearths. Churches stand pillaged and desecrated across the land. From that darkness, Arthur's story rises for young readers. Gilbert gives children the Round Table legends with their danger and wonder kept strong.
22561-tame-animals:
Tame Animals is a simple natural history book for young readers. It explains the farm and household animals children knew best. Cows come first in its plain, useful account of stock.

Cows are very useful to mankind, the book begins directly. They supply milk from which butter and cheese are made. Their young ones are called calves, young readers are told. The flesh of calves is veal, it adds without flinching. A good cow gives about fifteen or more quarts daily. Much depends on the quality of pasture she feeds upon. Such facts made the book a small farm primer. It teaches animal names, products, and care together.
22599-the-hindu-arabic-numerals:
David Eugene Smith wrote The Hindu-Arabic Numerals, a history of the number signs the world now uses. The catalog record gives no year. Smith, a noted historian of mathematics, traces how the digits traveled from India through the Arab world into European counting houses and classrooms.

The sample dives into scholarly detail, comparing letter sounds across alphabets as part of tracing how symbols and names moved between languages. Such care marks the whole book: inscriptions, manuscripts, and merchant practice all get weighed. Smith shows that a system now taken for granted was once a foreign novelty that spread slowly. Readers of math history will find a compact, learned account of our everyday numbers.
22699-pipefuls:
Christopher Morley wrote Pipefuls, a 1920 collection of his light essays, named for the pipe a reader might smoke through them. Morley, bookseller, novelist, and beloved columnist, made a career of small subjects treated with warmth. The contents list reads like a stroll through his city, from Manhattan anatomy to Brooklyn Bridge and a long lunch.

Other pieces hunt houses, ride a Fifth Avenue bus, confess the feelings of a human globule, and revisit Long Island. Morley writes as a friend talking across a desk, learned but never heavy. Pipefuls belongs to the golden age of the newspaper column, when an essay could be about nothing but a Sunday morning. It still charms readers who like their prose companionable.
22961-nell-of-shorne-mills:
Charles Garvice sets Nell of Shorne Mills ringing with music and temper. Someone is picking out Old Folks at Home on one string, and it is intolerable, one character bursts out, while he tries to check a wretched book. Put it down, Dick, he threatens, or I will come over and smash both of you.

Garvice was among the best-selling romance writers of his age, and Nell's story follows his proven pattern. A mill village, a heroine of spirit, crossed love, and hidden circumstances fill the chapters. His dialogue snaps, his settings glow, and his plots forgive almost everyone by the end. Modern readers meet here the popular novel in its Edwardian Sunday-best, built to be borrowed, devoured, and passed along.
23301-each-man-kills:
Each Man Kills is a tale touched by the supernatural. Its narrator admits to unease about the district Maria is bound for. That country is the realm of gypsies and fortune tellers, and the birthplace of many strange legends, which makes him watchful on her behalf.

Maria, he adds, claimed to be strongly psychic. She had foretold one or two things that were probably coincidence, such as the death of their parents. Even so, those hits made an impression on him, and he is hardly a believer. Readers get a story poised between doubt and dread, where prophecy refuses to stay a parlour trick.
326-steep-trails:
John Muir gathers twenty-four field pieces in this volume, written across nearly thirty years of western travel. The sketches first ran as letters and short articles, then were set in order by place and date. They range from California and Utah to Nevada, Oregon, Washington, and the Grand Canyon.

Muir walks Mount Shasta, bathes in Salt Lake, notes Mormon lilies, and climbs Mount Rainier in vivid, close detail. He watches forests, farms, dead mining towns, and river country with a naturalist's care. The book keeps the fresh feel of notes made on the trail, and it shows why Muir became a voice for wild land.
446-a-book-of-remarkable-criminals:
H. B. Irving profiles notorious killers and swindlers in this study of crime and motive. Charles Peace, Robert Butler, Derues, Dr. Castaing, Professor Webster, and the mysterious Mr. Holmes each get a full career, trial, and fall. Partners in crime, from the widow Gras to Eyraud and Bompard, close the set.

Irving writes as a lawyer and historian, weighing evidence, motive, and the law's slow net. He stresses how passion, greed, and pride tangle men in their own deeds. The book reads as both true crime and moral study, careful with facts and keen on why ordinary folk turn to murder.
771-biographical-notes-on-the-pseudonymo:
Charlotte Brontë wrote these short pieces to clear up a common error: that the works signed Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell came from one hand. She states plainly that three sisters wrote them, Currer being herself, Ellis being Emily, and Acton being Anne. The notice was prefixed to a reprint of Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

Brontë tells how the sisters chose male pen names, how their books were received, and how Emily and Anne lived and died. Her tone is proud and mournful, defending her sisters' fame while mourning their loss. The pieces are essential reading for anyone who wants the true story behind the Bell name, told by the sister who survived.
a-book-of-remarkable-criminals:
H. B. Irving wrote these true-crime lives of notorious offenders. The contents promise studies of Charles Peace, the burglar and murderer; Robert Butler of the Dunedin murders; the poisoners Derues and Dr. Castaing; Professor Webster; the mysterious Mr. Holmes; and a closing part on partnerships in crime, from the Widow Gras to the Fenayrou case and Eyraud and Bompard.

Irving's introduction argues that crime deserves serious study: the connection between motive and act, he writes, is as necessary to the jurist as to the student of human nature. Each life is then told as a narrative, from early years through trial and execution or decline. Irving, a lawyer's son steeped in famous trials, writes as an essayist rather than a sensation-monger, which gives the book its lasting place in crime writing.
a-book-of-scoundrels:
Charles Whibley profiles famous rogues of past centuries with open delight in their skill. His contents list Captain Hind, Moll Cutpurse, Jonathan Wild, Ralph Briscoe, and Gilderoy, then Jack Sheppard, Cartouche, George Barrington, Deacon Brodie, and Charles Peace. Each life is told from the records and old pamphlets.

Whibley pairs many of his rogues and draws parallels between them, thief against thief. He treats a masterly theft as a kind of dark art and writes with wit rather than moral horror. The chapters mix true history, anecdote, and shrewd character study. Readers who enjoy old London crime and highway romance will find a rich store here.
a-century-of-roundels:
Algernon Charles Swinburne fills a whole book with one small form: the roundel, a short poem with a refrain that returns like a bell note. This second edition of 1883, from Chatto and Windus, dedicates the volume to Christina G. Rossetti. The contents number the poems to a hundred, as the title promises.

In Harbour, The Way of the Wind, Had I Wist, Time and Life, and A Baby's Death stand among the early titles. A roundel on the death of Richard Wagner joins them. Two preludes are named for Lohengrin and Tristan. Swinburne makes the tight form sing of children, seasons, friendship, and grief. The book is a jewel box of Victorian lyric craft.
a-garland-for-girls:
A Garland for Girls, by Louisa May Alcott, gathers seven stories named for flowers, written, she says, for her own amusement during enforced seclusion. Alcott signed the preface in September 1887 and inscribed the book to R A Lawrence, her grateful friend. The flowers that were her solace in illness suggested the titles: May Flowers, Pansies, Water-Lilies, Poppies and Wheat, Little Button-Rose, and two more sprays of blossom.

The first tale opens in Boston, where six girls, descendants of Pilgrim Fathers as Alcott notes, form a club for mental improvement and call it the Mayflower Club. Each story in the garland ties a girl's work, pride, or kindness to its flower. Alcott writes for the readers who grew up with her: young women earning, helping, and deciding, with sentiment kept on a short stem and moralizing woven into incident rather than preached.
an-enquiry-concerning-the-principles-of-:
David Hume's Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals recasts his earlier moral philosophy in clearer form. Hume explains in his advertisement that the work restates ideas first printed in his Treatise of Human Nature. This edition follows the posthumous printing of 1777. The subject is why people praise some traits and blame others.

Sections treat benevolence, justice, and political society in turn. Hume argues that utility, meaning usefulness to people, explains much of our approval. Other chapters sort qualities that serve ourselves and qualities that please others at once. Four appendices handle moral sentiment, self-love, justice, and disputes over words. The book remains a founding text of modern ethics, valued for its calm tone and its test of moral rules against human feeling.
b09-brant-ship-of-fools:
Sebastian Brant, a Strasbourg lawyer, launched his Narrenschiff, The Ship of Fools, in German in 1494. The poem loads every kind of fool onto one ship bound for folly's land. Alexander Barclay turned it into English verse in 1509, and that rendering, in T H Jamieson's 1874 edition, fills this text.

Across 157 chapters Brant mocks greed, vanity, bad manners, false learning, and folly in church and state. Each fool gets a portrait in verse sharp enough to sting and broad enough to fit any age. The image of the ship sailed on through European art and letters, from Bosch to Bruegel. The satire still lands.
betty-wales-sophomore-a-story-for-girls:
Betty Wales, Sophomore, a story for girls, is credited on its title page to Margaret Warde. Warde's contents open with Moving In and Eleanor's Freshman. Parades and Parties, Points of View, and On Ambition carry the college year. The First Four, In the Argus Sanctum, and A Problem in Ethics raise the stakes toward midyears. Eva Nagel illustrated the 1905 volume.

Betty's sophomore year is the middle of a five book progress through college and beyond it. Freshman, junior, senior, and B A volumes stand around this one. The author's name on the title page is a pen name, and the series became a standard of girls' college fiction. Classes, the college paper, and friendship's ethics fill its world. No one fails out of Warde's college. The examinations that matter are social and moral, and Betty Wales passes them in a way meant to be copied.
biographical-notes-on-the-pseudonymous-b:
Charlotte Bronte wrote this biographical notice to end a mistake: readers believed Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell were one person. She states plainly that the Bells were three sisters, and that Ellis and Acton, Emily and Anne, were now dead. The notice prefaced a reprint of Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

Charlotte describes Emily's fierce, home-loving nature and Anne's quieter patience, borne through illness by firm Christian faith. She watched them, she writes, follow the same path at different steps toward early graves. A companion piece, her editor's preface, defends Emily's rough genius. Together these short pieces are essential documents for understanding the Bronte sisters and their chosen masks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acquaviva-car:
Acquaviva is the name of several Italian cardinals, and this entry sketches seven of them. Francesco, born at Naples in 1665 of the Dukes of Atri, served under four popes, was made cardinal and Bishop of Sabina by Clement XI, and died in 1723. Giovanni Vincenzo, Bishop of Melfi and Rapolla, became cardinal-priest in 1542 and died in 1566. Giulio, nuncio of Pius V to Philip II of Spain, was made cardinal by that pope and attended him on his deathbed.

Ottavio the elder, Archbishop of Naples in 1605, helped convert Henri IV. Ottavio the younger, made cardinal in 1654, served as legate in Viterbo and Romagna, curbing the banditti there. Troiano, made cardinal in 1732, represented the Spanish kings in the Curia and influenced the conclave electing Benedict XIV in 1740. Pasquale, made cardinal in 1773, closes the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-vessels:
Altar vessels centre on the chalice, holding the Eucharistic wine and water. It should be gold, or silver gilt inside, or a silver cup gilt inside with base and stem of any solid, clean, becoming metal. Stannum, a tin-lead alloy, is also allowed with a gilt interior. The paten, holding the altar bread, matches the chalice's material, gilt on its concave side if not gold, its edge thin and sharp to gather particles from the corporal.

The ciborium keeps consecrated particles for the laity's Communion, of any solid decent material, even gilt copper. The ostensorium, a glass-framed shrine of gold, silver, brass, or gilt copper, exposes the Blessed Sacrament publicly. A chalice loses consecration when unfit for use, as when the slightest break appears near the cup's bottom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angels:
Angel, from Latin angelus and Greek aggelos, from Hebrew for one going or one sent, means messenger. The Hebrew word means a divine or human messenger, rendered aggelos by the Septuagint, with both meanings. The Latin version distinguishes the spirit-messenger from humans, using angelus for the one and legatus or nuntius for the other. In a few passages the Latin version misleads, using angelus where nuntius would fit better, as in Isaiah 18:2.

Only the spirit-messenger concerns this article. It discusses the term's meaning, the angels' offices and names, good and evil spirits, the choirs, and appearances. Districts are allotted to angels termed their princes, as in the Apocalyptic angels of the seven churches. De Coelesti Hierarchia, ascribed to Saint Denis the Areopagite, treats of the hierarchies and orders of angels, though it dates centuries later. Its doctrine of the choirs has been received with extraordinary unanimity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-sch:
Apostolic schools are schools that train boys for the foreign missions, where the church is not yet normally organized. In settled lands, junior seminaries begin the training of diocesan clergy and theological seminaries complete it. Mission lands, by contrast, depend on foreign mission colleges and on apostolic schools to supply priests. Their object is to foster vocations, or calls to mission work, among youths who might otherwise never reach a seminary.

As distinct from junior seminaries, apostolic schools trace their origin to Father Alberic de Foresta, a Jesuit who lived from 1818 to 1876. He found many fine societies for prayer and mission funds, yet judged them weak without a supply of men to preach and give the sacraments. Experience in guiding souls convinced him that pious youths, held back by poverty or other bars, could still become missionaries if a school took them in hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appeals:
Appeals gives a comprehensive view of the church's positive law on appeals within the church court system. It leaves the nature of that court and the pope's right to receive appeals to other articles. An appeal is defined as a legal application to a superior authority for redress against an injury from a lower authority's act. The lower authority is called the judge from whom appeal is made, the higher the appellate judge or court. Appeals divide into judicial and extrajudicial kinds.

A judicial appeal attacks acts of the lower authority in its official role as judge at any stage of proceedings. It covers not only a final sentence but also an interlocutory sentence, one given during the case. The long article then works through kinds, effects, time limits, and procedure, giving canon lawyers and historians the full framework by which church judgments could be challenged and corrected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bath-and-well:
Bath and Wells is an ancient diocese coextensive with Somerset, England, though its first bishop under that exact title came only in 1244. Æthelhelm, later Archbishop of Canterbury, first ruled there from 909 to 914, choosing Wells's secular church as cathedral. Rivalry followed between Wells's secular canons and the monks of Glastonbury and Bath, with Wells struggling.

Bishop Gisa (1060-88) found Wells small and poor, its canons begging bread, and rebuilt it with lands from Edward, Harold, and William the Conqueror. His successor John de Villula undid much by moving the see to Bath in 1088, using its abbey as cathedral. Robert of Lewes (1136-66) rebuilt Wells's cathedral and arranged a settlement, and the diocese held three archdeaconries: Bath, Wells, and Taunton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bells:
Bells get a wide-ranging survey in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, treated in five parts that move from origins to law. The entry opens with ancient and early Christian uses of bells and sounding instruments, then turns to the rite of blessing them. That blessing, with its prayers and anointing, gives a bell its place in church life.

Later sections cover daily uses, from calling worshippers to marking deaths and alarms, and then inscriptions and old examples that survive. A closing part sets out points of canon law on who may bless, ring, and remove bells. The entry joins liturgy, craft, and church rule in one reference piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-kells:
The Book of Kells, an Irish manuscript of the Four Gospels, ranks as the choicest relic of Irish art. Also called the Book of Columba, it likely comes from Iona, and the Annals of Ulster record the theft of Columba's Gospel in 1006, probably this book. Tradition makes it Columba's own work, but its script and ornament place it no earlier than the late seventh or early eighth century.

Gerald of Wales saw it at Kildare in the twelfth century and praised it warmly. It later rested at Kells in Meath until 1541, and Archbishop Ussher gave it to Trinity College, Dublin, where it remains the library's treasure. Two unknown scribes seem to have written and painted it in black, red, purple, and yellow ink. Its spirals, trumpet patterns, beast interlacements, and ribbon plaits show Irish design at its inventive peak, though some ornaments stay unfinished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brussels:
Brussels, capital of Belgium, held 612,041 people at the end of 1905 with its eight suburban communes. It grew on the little Senne, now arched over by inner boulevards, and rose on the inland trade road between the Low Countries and Cologne. Canals link it to the Sambre and the Scheldt, and it has borne the title of seaport since 1895.

Tradition credits Saint Gery, Bishop of Cambrai, with a village and chapel on a Senne island late in the sixth century. First named Brosella, marsh dwelling, near the ninth century's end, it passed through Gerberga's dower to Lorraine's dukes. Charles of Lorraine made it his home and brought Saint Gudule's bones from Mortzelle in 979, making her the town's patron. On his son Otto's death in 1004, Lambert Balderic took Brussels, Vilvorde, and Louvain, seed of the duchy of Brabant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carolingian-s:
Carolingian schools grew from a Merovingian palace school, the scola palatina, that trained young Frankish nobles in war and court ceremony rather than letters. Literary teaching in those days belonged to monastic and cathedral schools. With Charlemagne's accession in 768, reform began in the palace school itself and spread by imperial decree to schools across his vast empire.

The palace school changed from tactics and manners to learning from 780, once victories over Lombards, Saxons, and Saracens allowed it. Real success came only with Alcuin's arrival at Aachen in 782. Alcuin headed the emperor's palace school and joined his council on all educational matters, becoming Charlemagne's prime minister of education and bringing York's learning tradition. Monastic, episcopal, and village schools carried the revival forward, despite war and pillage, to the dawn of university teaching in the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-summ:
A Catholic summer school gathers clergy and laity in the summer months for lectures and special courses, fostering intellectual culture in harmony with Christian faith along university-extension lines. The movement began with the Champlain Summer School. It was founded at New London, Connecticut, in 1892. In 1893 it settled permanently at Cliff Haven, New York.

Other schools followed. The Columbian Summer School opened at Madison, Wisconsin, in 1895, later moving to Milwaukee. A winter school began at New Orleans in 1896, and the Maryland Summer School in 1900. The article traces the roots of the movement in reading circles, university extension, and summer institutes, including Isaac Hecker's library work and the young men's lyceums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-mathi:
An entry on Charles Mathieu Schols, a Dutch civil engineer and geodesist, a measurer of the earth's surface, born at Maastricht in 1849. He trained at the Delft polytechnic, taught at the Royal Military Academy at Breda, and published a textbook on surveying in 1879. Offered the Delft chair of geodesy and surveying in 1878, he was elected to the Royal Academy of Sciences in 1880 and published a stream of papers on the mathematics of mapping.

Schols wrote on computing distance and direction from latitude and longitude, on joining small survey triangles to larger nets, and on map projections, the ways of flattening the curved earth onto paper. He also worked on error theory, pure mathematics, and bridge stresses, and he helped write a textbook on hydraulic architecture, the building of waterworks. He prepared and supervised the new national survey of Holland begun in 1886. He died at Delft in 1897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of the Pious Schools, also called Piarists and Scolopi, are a religious order founded at Rome in 1597 by Saint Joseph Calasanctius. A Confraternity of Christian Doctrine member, he taught country people and saw the need for early religious instruction of poor children. Antonio Brendoni, Santa Dorotea in Trastevere's pastor, gave him two rooms, soon joined by two other priests.

As attendance grew, Calasanctius moved the school into the city and lived there with companions. A later move to the Vestri Palace began community life, and Clement the Eighth approved the work with a yearly allowance for rent. Inspection by Cardinals Antoniani and Baronius satisfied critics, and Paul the Fifth approved still more warmly. On 25 March 1617 Calasanctius and his companions took the religious habit. Gregory the Fifteenth made the congregation a religious order on 18 November 1621.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cruelty-to-an:
A moral entry surveys attitudes to cruelty toward animals from pagan antiquity to Catholic doctrine. Pythagoras and Empedocles first urged kindness, holding that human souls pass into animal bodies after death, so animals share human rights. Cicero condemned that error, while Roman law still protected useful beasts.

The Old Testament forbade muzzling the treading ox and yoking ox and ass together. The New Testament is nearly silent, and the Fathers say little. Scholastics, above all St. Thomas, condemned needless suffering chiefly for its harm to the doer's character. Catholic doctrine, the entry argues, grants animals no rights yet denounces cruelty vigorously. Excessive fondness, it warns, is no sure index of moral worth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cure-of-souls:
A canon law entry defines the cure of souls, in Latin cura animarum, as a clerical office with a set district. Its holder teaches the faithful by sermons and warnings, and makes them holy through the sacraments, by lawful appointment. The pope holds it for the whole Church, bishops in their dioceses, and parish priests in their parishes.

Others share it under these leaders. Missionaries in lands without sees share the pope's care for those regions, and parish curates serve parts of a parish under their pastor. Its object is the salvation of souls, carrying on Christ's mission on earth. A priest's mission comes from the Church alone. It flows through apostolic succession in two forms: holy orders, passed on by bishops, and jurisdiction, passed on by the living teaching office headed by the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devotional-me:
A survey of devotional medals, pieces of metal struck or cast like coins but never used as money, bearing an image, device, or inscription for memory's sake. Religious medals outdo secular ones in variety. They mark persons, shrines, and events, first Communions and ordinations, and mysteries of faith. They teach piety, badge associations, protect the wearer, and carry indulgences.

Early Christian examples were long doubted. De Rossi's 1869 article settled some as genuine. The Middle Ages left little trace, and the Renaissance brought medals proper into popular post-Reformation use. Classes follow. Plague medals show Sebastian, Roch, and shrine views. Other medals mark Eucharistic miracles such as Seefeld, and private medals mark baptisms and weddings. Legend medals close the list, led by the cross said to have reached Saint Ulrich before battle in 955.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-christi:
Angels were seldom shown in Christian art before Constantine. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the oldest angel fresco, an Annunciation of the second century in the cemetery of Saint Priscilla. In the cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus, Wilpert found a third-century Annunciation, where Gabriel likewise appears as a human figure, robed in tunic and pallium. The Good Angel of a fourth-century fresco of the judgment of Vibia also wears human dress, as a sacred personage.

The winged angel, though Scripture offers ample warrant, does not appear before Constantine, likely because wings would recall favorite subjects of classical art. The entry then traces angels in litanies and churches, with Michael and Gabriel invoked just after the Trinity. Umbria was famed for angel churches, and the East raised many to Saint Michael.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical annals belong to the historical writing of the Middle Ages, classed with chronicles and lives of saints. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that chronicles began in Greece, while annals first appear among Romans. In the Middle Ages chronicle covered every form of history, though at first it meant only a chronological table. Pagan history no longer appealed to Christian writers, who sought a history centered on the kingdom of God.

To the new generation the heart of history lay in the misfortunes of the Jewish nation, a theme Roman historians ignored. Christians needed a general history in tune with their ideal. The entry follows the annal form from its Roman roots through Carolingian writers such as Einhard, with Kurze and Waitz among its guides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-san:
Episcopal sandals are low shoes, more like slippers, worn with liturgical stockings at pontifical solemn Mass. Unlike ancient sandals, mere soles tied by straps, they have a leather sole and an upper of silk or velvet, often embroidered. No cross is required on them, since at Rome that mark is a papal privilege alone. The stockings, called caligae, are silk, knitted or sewn.

Only bishops may wear sandals and caligae by right; abbots and other prelates need a special papal privilege. They are used only at pontifical Mass and ordinations, never at Confirmations or solemn Vespers. Their colour follows the day, but there are no black sandals or stockings, since they are not used at Masses for the dead or on Good Friday. They belong to the Latin rite alone and are unknown in Eastern rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernst-of-hess:
Ernst of Hesse-Rheinfels, a landgrave, was born on 9 December 1623 at Cassel and died on 12 May 1693 at Cologne. Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse-Cassel, was his father, and Ernst was his sixth son. Ernst and his brother Hermann founded the collateral lines of Hesse-Rheinfels and Hesse-Rotenburg after Moritz resigned the government in 1627 to his son Wilhelm V. His conversion to the Catholic Faith stirred controversial literature, and that is why he figures prominently in his country's religious history.

His mother raised him under strict discipline, and his instruction in the Reformed Church received the utmost attention. In 1642 he joined the Hessian army, where he proved an able commander of troops fighting on Sweden's side in the Thirty Years' War. While visiting the Hessian General Geyso, imprisoned at Gesecke, he was himself arrested and taken prisoner to Paderborn. Talk there with the royal army chaplain began his conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-espousals:
An espousal is a contract of future marriage between a man and a woman, who are thereby affianced. The law governing this contract was amended by the decree Ne Temere, published 2 August 1907 and effective 19 April 1908. For the old legislation see Betrothal; the present article is confined to the new. The decree enacts that only written espousals, signed by both parties and by the parish priest, the ordinary, or two witnesses, are valid and beget canonical effects.

If a party cannot write, this is noted, and another witness signs with the priest, the ordinary, or the two witnesses. Until Easter 1908 no written document was prescribed for espousals, except for Spain. Before, the promise of marriage bound the parties according to prevailing law or custom. That caused difficulties which necessitated this law. Private, clandestine espousals are henceforth of no value in the eyes of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelical-c:
The Evangelical Counsels, also called the Counsels of Perfection, are Gospel counsels for those who would do more than the bare minimum for heaven. Christ laid down precepts binding on all, above all the Ten Commandments, as the needful condition of eternal life. Beside them he taught counsels, not binding on all, for those aiming at Christian perfection as far as it can be reached on earth. Christ told the rich young man first to keep the commandments, then, if he would be perfect, to sell all and give to the poor.

The three chief counsels answer the three great goods of this world: riches, pleasures of the flesh, and honors. Poverty frees the soul from riches, chastity from fleshly pleasure, and obedience from self-love and rank. A soul may be saved without them, but reaches heaven more surely with them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-false-decreta:
The False Decretals are a forged set of papal letters from the ninth century. They circulated under the name of Isidore Mercator, or Pseudo-Isidore. The collection mixes genuine texts with about a hundred forged letters. Its three parts cover early popes, councils, and later decretal law.

Scholars exposed the forgery through anachronisms in dates, language, and law. Blondel's critique of 1628 proved decisive against the collection. The Ballerini brothers and Hinschius later produced critical editions of the texts. The article traces the forgery's spread and its effect on church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-fool:
The Feast of Fools was a licensed medieval revel held near New Year's Day. It grew from the subdeacons' festival on the Circumcision feast. Deacons, priests, and choristers each had their own December days. The subdeacons' day became a feast of the lower clergy and fools' guilds.

Its license echoed the pagan Saturnalia, when slaves stood equal to masters. Church authorities condemned its excesses again and again, often in vain. At Paris in 1199 the bishop curbed, but did not ban, the revel. The feast's core idea was brief reversal, with the lowly raised high.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-guar:
The Feast of Guardian Angels honours the angels assigned to each individual person. Local at first, it reached Cordova in 1579 and Toledo and Valencia soon after. Paul V placed it in the general calendar in 1608. Clement X later made it obligatory for the whole Church on 2 October.

The belief itself is ancient, though the feast is comparatively recent. Early liturgies already praised angelic protection and intercession for mortal men. The Mass texts stress the angels' threefold office of praise and guidance. In Germany the feast is kept on the first Sunday of September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-counc:
General Councils are lawfully convened assemblies of church leaders and theologians to settle doctrine and discipline by common deliberation. Council and synod mean the same, though mere worship meetings and diocesan synods fall short of the name, and unlawful gatherings earn the titles of robber synods. The entry defines the thing before it sorts its kinds.

Its heads run from classification and history through the pope's share in calling, guiding, and confirming councils, to who may sit, how many must come, and how business moves. The deepest questions close the work: whether councils err, how papal and conciliar infallibility fit, whether a council stands above the pope, and whether it can depose him. Definition, facts, and theory each get their turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-and-go:
Gospel and Gospels is a general article on the word Gospel, usually a written record of Christ's words and deeds. It likely comes from the Anglo-Saxon god, good, and spell, to tell. It matches the Greek euangelion, good tidings, and the Latin Evangelium. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets out the other meanings of euangelion in the body of the piece.

The first four historical books of the New Testament carry titles such as Euangelion kata Matthaion, which, however ancient, do not go back to the authors themselves. The Muratorian Canon, Clement of Alexandria, and Irenaeus witness to the headings in the latter part of the second century. Their early currency suggests they were prefixed in the first part of that century, once the four narratives were collected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace-at-meal:
Grace at Meals is an article on prayer at table from apostolic times, when Paul counseled doing all to the glory of God. Clement of Alexandria held it fitting to praise the Creator before nourishment and to sing his praises over the things created. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the ancient formulae behind the Roman Benedicite and Graces.

Tertullian shows third-century Christians signing the cross at table, praying before reclining, and closing the feast with prayer. Archaeology has found cup-bases reading Drink in Christ and Drink piously. One ancient formula, in a fourth-century treatise wrongly ascribed to Athanasius, thanks the Father for the Resurrection. It prays the scattered Church be gathered as bread is made one. In the Roman liturgy the Benedicite and Graces use Psalms 149 and 33, with Psalm 1 at midday and Psalm 116 in the evening.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace-before-:
Grace before Meals is an article on thanksgiving over food, where grace in pre-Elizabethan English always took the plural graces and means nothing but thanksgiving. Gratitude for bounty is not exclusively Christian, yet following the Saviour's own example the obligation was emphasized from the beginning. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces the practice from Paul and Aristides to the Breviary.

Paul gave thanks before eating in the sight of all. About 123 Aristides declared Christians render God thanks over food and drink. Tertullian wrote that prayer is tasted before the banquet and ends the feast, and Prudentius composed hymns Before Food and After Food. In religious orders the custom was much insisted on, with a section in Chapter 43 of Benedict's Rule, and schools and colleges kept their own metrical forms, some surviving today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-great-falls:
Great Falls is a diocese created by Pius X on 18 May 1904, covering eleven counties in eastern Montana over 94,158 square miles. Its titular city takes its name from the Missouri's falls, 533 feet in cascades yielding 340,000 horsepower, ranking next to Niagara in beauty and mechanical value. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a mission land turned manufacturing centre.

Father De Smet and companions first celebrated Mass in the territory at Fort Benton in 1850. Jesuits founded Indian missions as early as 1841. At Saint Peter's Mission, now the Ursuline mother-house of Montana, 2732 baptisms of Indians were recorded from 1855 to 1879. Cheap power feeds flour, plaster, and iron works and a smelter turning out over one hundred million pounds of copper a year, and the city ranks next to Butte in population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guardian-ange:
Catholic teaching on guardian angels holds that each soul has an angel charged with guarding it from birth. Yet the entry stresses that this has never been defined as an article of faith. It is, in St. Jerome's phrase, the mind of the Church. The belief itself runs through pagan antiquity, Babylonian monuments, and the writings of Menander, Plutarch, and Plotinus.

Scripture carries the doctrine from Old Testament guides and protectors, in Genesis, Exodus, Tobias, and Daniel, to the New Testament's sharper statements in Matthew and Hebrews. St. Thomas holds that only the lowest angelic orders serve as guardians, acting on senses and imagination but not on the will, while Scotus and Durandus allow any angel that rank. The guardians stay with us even after death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-nails:
The Holy Nails raise a long-debated question: was Christ crucified with three nails or four? Early medieval art strongly supports four nails, and some historical writers favour that view, though none earlier than Gregory of Tours. In the thirteenth century, western art began to show the feet placed one over the other and pierced by a single nail.

That three-nail view matches Nonnus, Socrates, and a poem attributed to Gregory Nazianzen. More recent criticism notes that the two earliest Crucifixion images show no nails in the feet at all. Ambrose and other early writers imply only two nails, and Ambrose says Helena had one nail made into a bridle for Constantine. The entry sifts art, texts, and relic claims with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-oils:
Holy oils, or olea sacra, are blessed oils whose symbolic meaning matches their natural uses. They sweeten, strengthen, and make supple, and the church uses them so in its rites. Liturgical blessing of oil is very ancient. Serapion's fourth-century Prayer Book and the Apostolic Constitutions show it, as does a Syriac document from the fifth or sixth century.

Serapion's book gives a formula for blessing oil and chrism for the newly baptized, when baptism and confirmation formed one ceremony. It gives separate blessings for oil of the sick, water, and bread. The prayer asks Christ to grant his creatures power for curing the sick, purifying souls, driving away impure spirits, and wiping out sins. Old Testament oil consecrated priests, kings, and altars, and served in sacrifices and purifications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitals:
Hospitals began as places where strangers or visitors were received, from the Latin hospes, a guest. Only over time did the word narrow to institutions for the care of the sick. That change tracks a long development under religious, political, economic, social, and scientific influences. The modern hospital, in this view, joins natural human care for suffering with Christian charity and medical skill.

Pagan antiquity already shows humane practice among civilized peoples, though some tribes killed the feeble. Princess Macha founded an early Irish hospital in 300 BC, and the Buddhist king Asoka set up hospitals for men and animals in 252 BC. The entry follows hospitals from those beginnings through Christian foundations, medieval houses, and modern scientific institutions across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infidels:
Those who have not been baptized are the people this entry calls infidels, from a Latin root meaning lack of faith. The name covers pagans who do not know the true God, and also Jews and Muslims, who worship God yet do not recognize Jesus Christ. Catechumens, still preparing for baptism, fall under the term in strict use, though early ages often called them Christians instead.

Baptized Christians outside the Catholic Church are not infidels in this language but non-Catholics. Baptism already makes a person a subject and child of the Church, even a rebellious one. The entry then maps how each group stands toward the Church and her laws. That distinction shaped mission policy, marriage rules, and the Church's claim over baptized persons everywhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-hessels:
Jean Hessels, a Louvain theologian born in 1522 and dead in 1566, taught eight years at Parc before taking the university theology chair. Like his senior colleague Baius, he drew theology from the Fathers, above all Augustine, rather than the Schoolmen, yet never strayed from received doctrine.

In 1559 Hessels went with Jansen and Baius to Trent, helped draft the decree on invoking saints, relics, and images, and faced Scholastic critics for leaving beaten paths. Back home he turned his energy against Protestants, defended the Immaculate Conception against Baius himself. He argued for papal infallibility in a work appended to his 1565 refutation of a new faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin-of-we:
Jocelin of Wells, bishop of Bath and Wells, died on 19 November 1242. Probably a Wells native, he acted as royal justiciar at Westminster in 1203, guarded vacant Lincoln, and held Wells canonry with two Herefordshire benefices. Sent by Savaric to force Glastonbury monks to drop a papal appeal, he later succeeded Savaric himself.

Elected bishop in February 1206 and consecrated at Reading that May, Jocelin fled the interdict in 1208, saw his estates seized, and regained them when John submitted in 1213. In 1215 he helped Langton win Magna Carta and stands named in it as royal counsellor. With Winchester's bishop he crowned boy-king Henry III, backed Hubert de Burgh against French forces, and served as travelling justice in the southwest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lateran-counc: A 1913 entry on the Lateran Councils — the papal synods. Henri Leclercq unfolds their fateful decrees. They ordered the medieval Church. Rome knew their mighty names. The centuries keep their canons. Their 1215 council is famed. Their 1512 council is famed. Their 1123 first council is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-kess: A 1913 entry on Kessels — the Dutch sculptor. Marie Louise Handley honors his marble heroes. His chisel graced the Roman halls. The age prized the gifted hand. The museums keep his art. His 1836 death is famed. His 1836 heroes are famed. His 1836 Roman marbles are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordeals: Ordeals were the ancient trials by fire, water, and combat that judged the accused when evidence failed. This entry traces their history, the Church's ambivalent role, and their abolition. Judgment by the elements: the Lateran Council finally forbade the clergy's part.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-fria: The Conventuals are the Franciscans who kept the great city convents and the corporate life. This entry traces their branch, its history, and its distinction from the Observants. The Franciscans of the cities: their great churches anchored the medieval towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-decreta: The decretals are the popes' great letters that built the canon law of the Middle Ages. This entry explains their collection, their authority, and their history. The common law of Christendom: their great collections filled the Church's five great books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacramentals: Sacramentals are the blessed objects and rites of the Church. This entry explains their kinds, their effects, and their use. The lesser signs of grace: their holy blessings aid the faithful in need and peril and sorrow and joy and peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-kel: The School of Kells was the monastery of the Meath plain. This entry covers its founder, its book, and its fame. The learning of the illuminated Gospels: its great book crowns the art in the 800s' scriptorium of the monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schools: Schools are the nurseries of the Catholic mind. This very long entry covers their history, their kinds, and their law. The training of the Christian youth: their crowded benches fill the lands in the 1900s' world of the Church in the nations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sioux-falls: Sioux Falls became the diocese of South Dakota. This entry covers its bishops, its churches, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the prairie state: its stone cathedral crowns the falls in Dakota's southeast in the county of Minnehaha.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th: The Helpers of the Holy Souls are the sisters of the purgatory. This entry covers their rule, their poor, and their houses. The daughters of the Paris foundress: their many poor fill the houses in the 1850s' decades in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spirituals: The Spirituals were the rigorists of the Franciscan order. This entry examines their poverty, their popes, and their end. The zealots of the strict observance: their fierce poverty split the order in the 1310s' Franciscans in the province of the Marches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paul-witho: St. Paul-Without-the-Walls is the basilica of the Apostle. This entry traces its Ostian Way, its fire, and its fame. The patriarchal church of the nations: its vast nave crowned Rome in the 300s of the empire in the city of the Caesars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stalls: Stalls are the carved seats of the choir. This entry traces their miserere, their making, and their churches. The furniture of the monastic office: their carved wood crowned the choir in the 1300s' abbeys in the stalls of the monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanley-falls: Stanley Falls was the mission of the Congo. This entry traces its fathers, its river, and its work. The station of the African apostolate: its new mission crowned the Congo in the 1890s' river in the falls of the Lualaba.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-angelical: The Angelicals were the congregation of Milan. This brief entry traces their Borromeo and their work. The sisters of the angelical life: their strict rule crowned Milan in the 1530s' convents in the city of the truly very old Ambrosians.
condensed-novels:
Bret Harte's first Condensed Novels squeezed famous fiction into a few pages each, and the joke made his early reputation. Handsome Is as Handsome Does mocks Charles Reade's manner, disposing of whole families in numbered lists. Muck-a-Muck travesties James Fenimore Cooper's frontier novels, Miss Mix sends up Charlotte Brontë, and The Ninety-Nine Guardsmen reduces Dumas's musketeers to manageable absurdity.

Wilkie Collins, Bret Harte's contemporaries, and a southern novel after Belle Boyd all get the treatment, names dashed out in the contents and styles copied to the life. Harte wrote these as a young California editor. They remain funny because the imitation is exact: every tic of plot, diction, and sentiment stands exposed in miniature.
courts-and-criminals:
Arthur Train's Courts and Criminals gathers essays written between 1905 and 1910, reprinted, he notes, without revision. Train served as a New York prosecutor, and the first essay attacks the pleasant fiction of the presumption of innocence. A young man named Duffy, photographed and measured by police without charge, opens the argument. The mayor, a judge, and a commissioner fight over his treatment.

Chapters move through the courts as Train worked them: police methods, juries, lawyers, and the machinery of prosecution. He writes with a practitioner's impatience for legal pieties and a storyteller's eye for the case that proves the rule. The essays argue for common sense against both brutality and sentimentality. Train later created Mr. Ephraim Tutt, fiction's beloved old lawyer. Here the material is real, and the insider's candour still startles: an American district attorney explaining, in public, how justice actually worked.
dead-souls:
Nikolai Gogol's Dead Souls, translated by D J Hogarth with an introduction by John Cournos, follows the smiling traveler Chichikov buying dead serfs, souls still listed on census rolls, from provincial landowners. The file contains the complete first part and the surviving fragment of the second, which Gogol partly burned. His preparer's note explains the missing pages honestly.

Manilov, the box-like Korobochka, the liar Nozdrev, and the miser Plyushkin, who read every book with equal empty attention, form a gallery of Russian provincial types. Chichikov's scheme is both fraud and mirror. Gogol meant a Dante-like trilogy of fall and redemption; what survives is the funniest and saddest portrait of his Russia ever written.
doe-osti-17038113-testing-machine-learni: Machine-learned implosion models got stress-tested, and this DOE report covers testing ML physics models of fusion performance. The pages record the trials. The modelers get their verdict. The models were tested. The trials were fusion. The verdict was recorded.
doe-osti-2997807-engineered-colloidal-he: Sunlight-to-hydrogen crystals got engineered, and this DOE report brews the nano cocktail. The pages detail the light-driven chemistry. The chemists get their data. The cocktail was colloidal. The chemistry was light-driven. The data were chemist. The cocktail was nano.
doe-osti-2998668-slia-reference-architec: SLIA got its reference architecture, and this DOE text models the system design. The pages detail the architecture. The engineers get their blueprint. The models were reference. The design was system. The engineers got blueprints. The blueprint was engineer. The design was system.
doe-osti-2999153-education-for-pv-modeli: Solar number-crunchers got their workshop lessons, and this DOE report shares the 2025 PVPMC takeaways. The pages detail what worked. The solar modelers get their notes. The lessons were workshop. The notes were modeler. The takeaways were solar. The report was DOE's.
doe-osti-3004386-tunable-few-layer-van-d: Van der Waals crystals got tuned, and this DOE final covers few-layer heterostructures. The pages detail the energy findings. The quantum folks get their closeout. The crystals were van der Waals. The closeout was quantum. The materials were emerging.
doe-osti-3006643-properties-of-electroni: Chip stuff and its specs got their DOE cheat sheet, and this text tables the electronic numbers. The pages detail the material data. The engineers get their reference. The cheat sheet was electronic. The sheet was DOE's. The numbers were material.
doe-osti-3377975-nuclear-security-risks-: HALEU got security-risked, and this DOE text covers fuel risks. The pages detail the nuclear findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The fuels were HALEU. The data were nuclear. The HALEU were risks. The nuclear were folks. The fuels were risks.
doe-osti-3453386-education-for-pv-modeli: PV modelers got education-surveyed, and this DOE text covers professional educator surveys. The pages detail the education findings. The energy folks get their data. The professionals were modeling. The data were energy. The survey were educators. The modeling were PV.
doe-osti-3625672-semi-transparent-perovs: Perovskites got tandem-stacked, and this DOE final covers semi-transparent solar cells. The pages detail the stacked findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The research was cooperative. The closeout was energy. The tandem were module. The cells were solar.
english-literature-for-boys-and-girls:
English Literature for Boys and Girls, by H E Marshall, tells the story of English writing as a chain of tales young readers can follow. Marshall opens in what she calls the listening time, before books, with the Irish cattle raid of Cooley and the sorrows of storytelling. Chapters move through King Arthur, Beowulf, and Caedmon, the father of English song, then to Bede, the father of English history.

Alfred the Great fights with his pen, Chaucer appears as bread and milk for children, and the Canterbury Tales get three chapters of inn and pilgrims. Later headings promise the first English guide book, the Bruce in Scotland, a poet king, the mystery plays, and Everyman. Marshall writes literary history as biography and adventure, trusting story to carry fact. Generations of children first met their national literature through her voice.
esther-a-book-for-girls:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's Esther is a book for girls, told in the first person by its heroine. Esther begins by confessing that she was always sorry her name was Esther, a small vexation that opens a long story of home, school and growing up.

Chapters follow her last day at Redmayne House, her arrival at Combe Manor, the old house at Milnthorpe, and life at the Brambles. Dot, Uncle Geoffrey, Miss Ruth, smugglers' caves, a long night and a brave deed carry the plot toward its sunset close. Carey writes with the warmth and moral steadiness that made her a favourite with Victorian girls, and modern readers will find Esther an engaging period heroine.
familiar-spanish-travels:
William Dean Howells's Familiar Spanish Travels records his travels in Spain, illustrated and published by Harper and Brothers in 1913. Howells begins with autobiographical approaches, recalling how a train toward Granada on a November evening in 1911 brought back an Ohio village of the 1850s.

Chapters follow San Sebastian and Biscay, Burgos and its bitter cold, Valladolid, Madrid, a night and day in Toledo, Cordova, Seville, Granada, Ronda, Algeciras and Tarifa. Howells writes as a familiar, companionable traveller, noting manners, buildings and daily life rather than Baedeker facts. Readers planning a Spanish journey, or revisiting one, will find his account warm and observant.
fundamental-principles-of-the-metaphysic:
Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, by Immanuel Kant and translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, lays out Kant's account of duty. Kant dates the work 1785 and begins by sorting philosophy into physics, ethics, and logic. Ethics, the science of the laws of freedom, is his ground here: what a rational person ought to do, apart from what custom or reward suggests.

Across its sections Kant moves from ordinary moral judgment to his central test. An act has true moral worth, he argues, when it is done from duty, not from liking or gain. The rule for action must be one the actor could will as a law for everyone, the test later called the categorical imperative, meaning an unconditional command of reason. Abbott's English made this short, hard book a standard text for students of philosophy in Britain and America.
general-history-for-colleges-and-high-sc:
P. V. N. Myers's General History for Colleges and High Schools compresses the story of the world into a single school volume. Myers bases the book on his earlier Ancient History and his Mediaeval and Modern History, changing the perspective and proportions where a one-volume survey required it.

The narrative runs from the ancient East through Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages and modern Europe, with the frontispiece showing the Attic plains and the Acropolis of Athens. Myers says he took the greatest care to verify facts and to report the newest finds and judgments of scholars, while admitting that so wide a range invites error. Teachers and students will find it a solid, old-fashioned survey, built for classroom use.
glenloch-girls:
Grace M. Remick's Glenloch Girls opens its series with a pleasant winter, says the introduction, in the lives of everyday girls and boys. Ruth Shirley expects to be very forlorn; instead, a new home in Glenloch welcomes her. The kindest of friends make her a Glenloch girl in heart and name. Ruth's Father, the first chapter, starts her story.

Three chums, a newcomer, and a new club follow: the Social Six is formed. Caps and aprons, Charlotte's problems, and Christmas presents fill the winter's small events. A boy among them learns patience when what he most prizes is taken away. Remick lists the sequels on her title page — Abroad, the Girls' Club, and Camp West — as promises. The book is wholesome series fiction of its period: friendship as curriculum, faults confessed, and good times earned. Glenloch's snow is the setting; the girls' loyalty is the plot.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pistols_Pistols: Special Agent Jack A. French of the FBI's Dallas office wrote this memorandum about a telephone tip. The caller was Tony Jackson of Fort Worth. His tip concerned Lee Harvey Oswald. Tips flooded the Dallas office after the assassination, and each one was written up whether it led anywhere or not. The file gives the agent, the caller, and the subject. It does not preserve what Jackson reported, so the tip itself cannot be described.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Referrals_Refer:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum about a withheld record. The FBI had referred material elsewhere and withheld Orest Pena's passport information from headquarters file 105-82555. Weisberg's point is sharp: the same information was already in the public domain, printed by the Warren Commission.

Pena was a New Orleans bar owner whose name runs through the Oswald inquiry. A passport detail about him, public in one place and withheld in another, was the kind of absurdity Weisberg collected. The memo argues that referral withholding had become a habit, not a judgment. It preserves the file number, the man's name, and the contradiction, a small clean example of secrecy outliving its reason.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WLS_WLS: Harold Weisberg wrote to Merrill Mazuer at WLS-TV in Chicago on April 30, 1970. Letters to television staff were a steady part of Weisberg's campaign against the Warren Commission report. He pressed broadcasters to cover his findings and answer his charges. The WLS letter shows that campaign reaching a major Chicago station, in Weisberg's direct and persistent style.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Le:
A car bomb in Washington, D.C. killed former Chilean ambassador Orlando Letelier and Ronni Moffitt on September 21, 1976. In the months after the attack, four State Department officers used a formal Dissent Channel memo to push their own government. This briefing book, posted in September 2019, publishes that declassified memo.

The officers wrote that President Augusto Pinochet probably ordered the assassination himself. They urged an aggressive policy to end normal relations with Chile and force him from power. Their protest failed at the time, but the memo shows dissent inside the State Department in plain, official language.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Signals intelligence, the interception of communications, caused turf wars inside American spying for decades. Jeffrey T. Richelson compiled this briefing book, number 506, published in March 2015. Its core is a formerly top-secret, multi-volume CIA history of that fight.

The history details CIA conflicts with the National Security Agency and the military over who owned the signals mission. Added documents describe CIA signals work at home and abroad, often in direct competition with NSA. Later cooperation between the rivals made possible the exploits that Edward Snowden exposed.
